title: Legal text becomes interface rules
subtitle: How the child design codes I coded turn a concern about harm into a concrete interface requirement

rows.harm: Compulsive use that disrupts sleep, eating, or learning
rows.rule: No push notifications to minors late at night or during school hours

rows.harm: Contact and exposure to adults a child does not know
rows.rule: Minors are not visible to, or contactable by, unconnected adults by default

rows.harm: Engagement features that keep children using a service
rows.rule: Engagement counts (likes, views) hidden by default
A visible signal whenever someone, including a parent, is monitoring
rows.where: New Jersey, Vermont (Maryland does not require one)

rows.harm: Recommendations the user did not ask for
rows.rule: Recommend only from preferences the user stated; disclose the inputs used
Collect the minimum needed for age assurance and delete it after use

caption: Each row pairs a harm with the design rule a law uses to address it. Whether children can find, understand, and use these controls is not something the laws themselves test.
source: Coding of the UK Age Appropriate Design Code and five U.S. state laws (MD, NE, SC, NJ, VT), UIUC iSchool, 2026. Preliminary.
